Asymptotically optimal path planning with an
approximation of the omniscient set
Jon´aˇs Kˇr´ıˇz, Vojtˇech Von´asek
Abstract—The asymptotically optimal version of Rapidly-
exploring Random Tree (RRT*) is often used to find optimal
paths in a high-dimensional configuration space. The well-known
issue of RRT* is its slow convergence towards the optimal
solution. A possible solution is to draw random samples only
from a subset of the configuration space that is known to contain
configurations that can improve the cost of the path (omniscient
set). A fast convergence rate may be achieved by approximating
the omniscient with a low-volume set. In this paper, we propose
new methods to approximate the omniscient set and methods
for their effective sampling. First, we propose to approximate
the omniscient set using several (small) hyperellipsoids defined
by sections of the current best solution. The second approach
approximates the omniscient set by a convex hull computed
from the current solution. Both approaches ensure asymptotical
optimality and work in a general n-dimensional configuration
space. The experiments have shown superior performance of our
approaches in multiple scenarios in 3D and 6D configuration
spaces.
The proposed methods will be available as open-source on
https://github.com/BipoaroXigen/JPL.
Index Terms—Motion and Path Planning; Planning, Schedul-
ing and Coordination
I. INTRODUCTION
T
HE task of optimal path planning is to find a collision-
free path with the lowest cost (e.g., path length) from a
start configuration to a goal configuration. Low-dimensional
configuration spaces can be discretized, and the optimal path
can be searched using, e.g., A*. Sampling-based motion plan-
ners, e.g., Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) [1], search
the configuration space using randomized sampling, and they
are more suitable for searching high-dimensional spaces than
the discretization methods. RRT* [2] is an asymptotically
optimal variant of the RRT algorithm. RRT* continues the
search even after the first feasible solution is found. Moreover,
RRT* uses a rewiring technique to optimize node connection
within the tree, so the costs of the nodes decrease with the
increasing number of samples. The rewiring process relies on
nearest-neighbor search, and it becomes more computationally

RRT* samples the whole configuration space (Fig. 1a),
which is not necessary, as there exist states that cannot possibly
improve the existing solution. This was first observed in [3]
where the “omniscient set” is defined. The omniscient set is
a subset of the configuration space suitable for finding the
optimal solution. In obstacle-free environments, it has a form
of prolate n-dimensional hyperellipsoid. Drawing samples
only from the hyperellipsoid has been shown to improve the
convergence towards the optimal solution. However, for long
zig-zag paths, the volume of the hyperellipsoid may still be
too large, which causes Informed-RRT* to perform similarly
as RRT* (Fig. 1a,b).
In this paper, we propose two approaches to approximate the
omniscient set. The first proposed approach employs multiple
small hyperellipsoids defined by subsections of the current
best solution (Fig. 1c). This set ensures asymptotic optimality.
The second approach computes a convex hull of a path rotated
along a line from start to goal (Fig. 1d). Finally, we combine
these two approaches and show how to achieve asymptotic

II. RELATED WORK
The family of sampling-based planners attempts to solve
the path planning problem by randomized sampling of the
configuration space. A popular method is RRT [1], and its
variants [6], [7]. The original RRT provides a feasible solution,
but it cannot guarantee finding the optimal solution.
In [2], asymptotically optimal sampling-based planners
RRT* and PRM* were proposed. In RRT*, the connection
of the tree’s nodes is optimized using a rewiring procedure
to achieve near-optimal solutions. In contrast to basic RRT,
where the tree growth is terminated if it reaches the goal con-
figuration, RRT* continues to grow (and rewire) the tree even
after the first feasible solution is found. Various improvements
of RRT* were proposed: a) methods changing the sampling
distribution, b) using multiple trees, c) improved rewiring
procedures, and d) other techniques focusing on low-level
routines. The surveys [8], [6], [9], [10] cover the contributions
to the field of asymptotically optimal motion planning.
Adapting the sampling distribution. The original RRT* sam-
ples the (whole) configuration space. As was shown in [11],
[3], not all configurations can improve the quality of the
existing solution. Therefore, the sampling can be made within
a subset of the configuration space. In Informed-RRT* [3],
the authors define a set of configurations that can improve
the path cost. Generally, this set is an n-dimensional prolate
hyperspheroid. After the initial feasible solution is found,
the random samples are generated from this subset. This
reduces the volume of space to be sampled and improves
the convergence rate. The BIT* planner [5] processes the
samples of the hyperspheroid in batches: random samples
are generated in the given area and processed (i.e., used for
tree expansion) in the order given by a chosen heuristic.
Cloud RRT* [12] decomposes the search space by a set of
spheres with various priorities and uses the spheres to generate
random samples. Initially, the spheres are computed using a
Generalized Voronoi Graph of the workspace and updated if
a new, better path is found.
The work [13] employs a Convolutional Neural Network
(CNN) to provide the sampling distribution. CNN is trained
on a 2D map where optimal paths are computed using A*, but
due to representing the map as an RGB image, the method [13]
is limited only to 2D configuration spaces. The works [14],
[15] proposed to steer the new nodes of RRT* towards the
goal using the Potential Field method. In [16], the sampling
distribution is learned using a variational autoencoder from
a set of successful motion plans. The learned distribution
improves the convergence rate of BIT*. The work [17] uses
the Gaussian Mixture model to learn the sampling distribution
from human-demonstrated trajectories. RRT# [18] is a two-
stage planner: exploration, which captures the topology of the
space and extends the tree, and exploitation, which attempts
to improve the current solution. Nodes having the potential to
be a part of the optimal solution are estimated using available
knowledge about the cost of the best path and cost-to-come
values, which allows to focus the sampling to promising
regions of the configuration space.
RRT* with multiple trees. RRT*-Connect employs the bidi-
rectional search [19]: two trees are grown (from the start and
goal), both in the RRT* manner, and a new node extending
one tree is also tested for extending the other tree. The
work [20] combines Informed-RRT* with the bidirectional
search [20]. The bidirectional IB-RRT [21] estimates the best
tree (and its best node) where to insert the random samples.
The work [22] is based on BIT* and uses the bidirectional
backward and forward search. The backward search is fast
as it checks collisions approximately, and its purpose is to
estimate the heuristic. On the contrary, the forward search
checks the collisions fully, grows in the BIT* manner, and uses
the heuristic from the backward search. The forward search
informs the backward search about invalid (colliding) edges,
so the heuristic is updated during the search.
RRT* with improved rewiring. In RRT*, parents for the
newly added node are vertices in the hypersphere around
the new node. Quick-RRT*[23] extends this set also to the
ancestors of these vertices. F-RRT* [24] further extends this
idea by creating new parent nodes instead of selecting them
amongst nodes in the tree. T-RRT* [25] extends RRT* by the
transition test to prefer extension by nodes with lower costs.
Improving low-level routines. RRT* performs a vast amount
of collision checks, which can be computationally intensive.
The paper [26] proposed to perform collision detection of
edges only if a new path is computed. The work [27] as-
sociates obstacle proximity information with each node, and
collision detection is computed only if the nearest neighbor
is too far or if the node is close to obstacles. In memory-
efficient RRT* [28], authors limit the maximum size of the
tree, which is achieved by removing provably useless nodes
every time a new node is added to the tree. The authors
of [4] extend RRT* for the purpose of online path planning.
Besides the standard Euclidean metric, the work [4] employs a
second assistive metric that helps to improve the convergence
rate. An extension of the node expansion for kinodynamic
systems without a BVP (Boundary Value Problem) solution
was proposed in [29]. The tree is propagated using the forward
system simulation. Moreover, the nodes are pruned based on
their cost, which reduces the size of the trees and speeds up
the nearest neighbor search.
In this paper, we focus on adapting the sampling space.
The most relevant work is the Informed RRT* [3], [11] which
defines the sampling space as a hyperellipsoid guaranteed to
contain the optimal path. The hyperellipsoid is parametrized by
the best (shortest) path found so far. The downside of [3] is that
when the current shortest path is too wiggly, the hyperellipsoid
may be even bigger than the whole free configuration space.
We propose several techniques to approximate the omniscient
set [11] and to focus the sampling to more relevant regions of
the configuration space, as is demonstrated in Fig. 2.

III. PROBLEM FORMULATION
Let C denote the configuration space, and let Cfree ⊆C
denote the free region where the robot can move. A path
P = (p1, p2, . . . , pn), pi ∈C is a sequence of configu-
rations. A subsection of the path is defined as a sequence
Pj,k = (pi), i = j, . . . , k, pi ∈P. The length of the path P
is denoted len(P), and it corresponds to the sum of distances
between path elements Pn
i=2 ||pi−1 −pi||.
The task is to find the optimal (i.e., minimizing len(P))
collision-free path Popt = (pi), pi ∈Cfree from the start
configuration qstart ∈Cfree to the goal region Qgoal ⊆C,
i.e., p1 = qstart and pn ∈Qgoal. In the rest of the paper, n
refers to the cardinality of P.
IV. THE MOTIVATION BEHIND PROPOSED METHODS
The original RRT and RRT* algorithms sample the whole
configuration space C uniformly. We define the sampling space
S ⊆C as the region from which the random samples are drawn
(i.e., in RRT and RRT*, S = C). As was shown in [11], only
a subset of the configuration space contains samples that can
possibly improve the cost of the path P (and it is guaranteed
that samples outside this set cannot improve the cost of the
path P). This set is called the “omniscient set” O:
O = {q| len(Pto) + len(Pfrom) ≤len(P); q ∈C},
(1)
where Pto is a path from qstart to a configuration q and Pfrom
is a path from a configuration q to qgoal. The lengths of the
paths can be approximated with a heuristic. The Euclidean
distance heuristic would lead to the “informed set” Si, which
is a prolate hyperellipsoid
Si = {q| ∥qstart −q∥+ ∥q −qgoal∥≤len(P); q ∈C}. (2)
To improve the length of the path, it is sufficient to draw
random samples only from the informed set Si, as no con-
figurations outside Si can improve the cost of the path. This
is the core of Informed-RRT* [3], [11] which draws random
samples only from Si, and where the set Si is defined using
the length of the current best path.
However, the volume of Si can still be quite high (especially
for long zig-zag paths), which is depicted in Fig. 2. Moreover,
it is not guaranteed that all configurations from the informed
set Si can improve the path.

The smaller the volume of S, the less time will be spent
sampling non-improving configurations. Ideally, the sampling
space would be exactly the desired optimal path (i.e., S =
Popt). However, Popt is not known in advance.
To reduce the number of samples that do not improve the
solution, we propose several approaches to approximate the
omniscient set O, and we propose methods for their sampling.
V. LOCALLY INFORMED SAMPLING SPACE
The first proposed sampling space is a modification of Si
of Informed-RRT* [3]. Instead of constructing a hyperellip-
soid from the whole path, many smaller hyperellipsoids are
constructed from various subsections of the path. Each path
subsection Pj,k has a corresponding hyperellipsoid sj,k:
sj,k = {q| (∥q −pj∥+ ∥q −pk∥) ≤len(Pj,k); q ∈C; }, (3)
sj,k constructed in this manner is guaranteed to contain the
shortest path from pj to pk as proven in the original Informed-
RRT* paper [3], section III.
The Locally Informed Sampling Space, which we will
denote Sl, is the union of all local hyperellipsoids sj,k, which
satisfy constraints given by the parameter c, 2 ≤c ≤n:

The parameter c controls the explore-exploit tradeoff. With
the parameter c = n, sampling from Sl is equivalent to
sampling from Si (i.e., in the same manner as in the Informed-
RRT* planner). High values of c lead to exploration, as
the set Sl contains only the larger hyperellipsoids, and it
supports the discovery of new alternative optimal solutions.
In contrast, with the low values of c, the set Sl contains more
small hyperellipsoids (computed from path subsections Pj,k
of cardinality at least c), which leads to the exploitation of the
current best solution (i.e., smoothing). Setting the parameter c
high (close to the n of the initially found path) can lead to a
premature halt of the smoothing and the use of Si on a path
not yet smoothed out.
In the following subsection, we show how to efficiently sam-
ple Sl without explicitly constructing all the hyperellipsoids,
which would be computationally very demanding.

VI. CONVEX SAMPLING SPACE
The second proposed sampling space is obtained as a convex
hull of revolution of P around the axis connecting qstart and
qgoal (we refer to this axis as the SG-axis (start-goal-axis) in
the rest of the paper) (Fig. 4a, 4b). We denote this sampling
space as Sc. Computing Sc of the rotated path (a convex
hull of an infinite set) would be complicated and unnecessary.
Since the resulting hull is axially symmetric along the SG-
axis, we can utilize that knowledge to represent Sc by a two-
dimensional slice.
We can define a “slice” of the convex hull, which is an
intersection of Sc and a plane going through the SG-axis
(Fig. 4c). Such a slice is two-dimensional, allowing us to
represent Sc in 2D. A point inside the slice can be represented
by the distance along the SG-axis and the distance from the
axis to the point. Defining the slice and its coordinate system
enables us to generate random points inside Sc by first drawing
a random sample inside the slice and then distributing the
sample into the volume of Sc.
Let A be the orthogonal projection matrix onto the SG-axis.
For a configuration q ∈C, we define the distance along the
SG-axis a(q) and the distance from the axis f(q) as

A. Slice computation
We project each configuration pi of the path P onto the
SG-axis using A and denote the first and the last projected
configurations o and t, respectively (the projections are ordered
by their scalar projection on the SG-axis, i.e., according to
their distance a(·) along the axis). Note that transf(o) =
(0, 0). The coordinate system of the slice is depicted in Fig. 5.
Computation of the slice. Let transf(P ∪{o, t}) denote
a set of 2D points obtained by applying the transformation to
each point of the path P and to the points o and t. As all
these points now lie on a 2D plane, we can compute their 2D
convex hull and obtain the set of extremal points of the hull
that we denote V . The points vi ∈V then define the shape
(polygon) of the slice, and the whole Sc would be achieved
by rotating this polygon around the SG-axis. Computing the
2D convex hull of m points (here, m = n + 2, i.e., number
of waypoints plus two points o and t) has time complexity
O(m log m). Practically, the method can be slightly sped up.
Efficient computation of the slice. The efficient compu-
tation of the convex hull of the slice points is based on a
modified Graham scan [30]. Graham scan decides whether
the point lies within the hull (and therefore can not be an
extremal point) by checking whether three consecutive points
form a right or a left turn.
We modify the Graham scan using prior knowledge about
the resulting hull of the set of points V = transf(P ∪{o, t}).
First, one edge of the convex hull is already known (it is the

C. Drawing random samples from Sc
We can sample the set Sc either directly or with rejection
sampling. The rejection sampling approach is simple to imple-
ment but less efficient for high dimensional C or if the volume
of Sc is low (in comparison to the volume of the whole C).
Sampling Sc in higher dimensions (or when the volume of Sc
is low) can be efficiently achieved using the direct sampling.
Rejection Sampling of Sc. Let r ∈C be a random sample
from C, and v′ = transf(r). We accept the sample r as being
in Sc if the point v′ is located inside the 2D convex hull of
the slice.
Direct sampling of Sc. First sample a′ from interval [0, ∥o−
t∥] (see definitions in subsection VI-A), the sampling should
be weighted by fmax (2fmax is the width of the slice of Sc
for a given value of a(·)) at each a′. The sampled value of a′
determines the maximal value fmax that f ′ can obtain. Then,
sample f ′ uniformly from the interval [0, fmax]. This forms a
random sample g = (a′, f ′). The random configuration q ∈C
is computed as: q = a′ ⃗d + f ′⃗r, where ⃗d is a unit vector in
direction from qstart to qgoal, and ⃗r is a random unit vector
perpendicular to ⃗d. The reconstruction process is illustrated in

VII. LOCALLY INFORMED CONVEX SAMPLING SPACE
The previously defined sampling spaces Sl and Sc can be
combined; this leads to another sampling space Scl = Sl ∩Sc.
While Sc will bring down the volume of the sampling space,
Sl will put more weight on sampling in the proximity of the
found path, locally smoothing out the fast converging solution.
Example of the space Scl is depicted in Fig. 7.
Fig. 7: An intersection of Sc and Sl, denoted as Scl.
A. Drawing random samples from Scl
To draw a random sample from Scl, first a random sample
is generated in Sl (which is described in section V-A), and the
sample is accepted only if it is also located in Sc (which is
realized using the Alg. 3).
VIII. DISCUSSION
The proposed approximations of the omniscient set and
methods for their sampling can be integrated into any RRT*-
based planner (instead of drawing random samples from the


6
whole C, the planner draws random samples from Sl, Sc or
Scl). Similarly to Informed-RRT*, where the set Si is updated
when a new (shorter) path is found, the proposed sets Sl, Sc,
and Scl can be updated every time a new path is found.
Sampling from Sl (Section V-A) is computationally not
demanding. It only requires selecting a subsection of the
current best solution and defining the hyperellipsoid using its
first and last configurations. Therefore, sampling from Sl has
the same complexity O(1) as sampling in Informed-RRT*.
Drawing random samples from Sc (and also from Scl) is
computationally more demanding. Every time a new solution
is found, it is required to apply transformation in Eq. 6 to
all points of the current best solution P and to compute the
convex hull as described in section VI-C. The time complexity
of the convex hull computation is O(n log n) for a path P
with n waypoints. More frequent hull reconstruction will result
in a faster decrease of Sc volume. However, reconstructing
the hull too often can slow down the planning, without
much improving the convergence. We observed that it is not
necessary to construct Sc every time the current best solution
is improved, but it is satisfactory to update it in every m
iterations (in our experiments, we used m = 1, 000).
The locally informed sampling space Sl enables more
frequent sampling close to the current best-known path. The
planners using Sl tend to have a faster convergence rate
than ones using Sc in environments where less topologically
distinct paths are present (for example, the Hard, Comb,
and 3Dcomb environments) and slower in the opposite case.
The Scl can be used as a compromise when there is not
enough information about the environment. Sampling from Sl
preserves asymptotic optimality.

On the contrary, the spaces Sc and Scl do not guarantee to
fully cover the omniscient set as Si and Sl do, and drawing
random samples only from these would result in a planner that
does not ensure asymptotic optimality. Therefore, to ensure
asymptotic optimality when using Sc or Scl, random samples
should also be generated from Si with a non-zero probability.
This is an often adopted trick that combines Informed-RRT*
(which samples from Si) with other methods because the
combination preserves asymptotic optimality.

In all tested 2D and 3D environments, the proposed methods

X. CONCLUSION
The well-known issue of asymptotically optimal path plan-
ning using RRT* is its slow convergence towards the optimal
path. In this paper, we have proposed novel methods to approx-
imate the omniscient set, i.e., the subset of the configuration
space that is known to contain samples that can improve the
quality of the path. The first proposed approach uses multiple
hyperellipsoids that are defined by a subsection of the current
best path. In the second approach, we construct a convex
hull of the current best path. We describe how to sample
these spaces. The proposed methods can be integrated into
any RRT*-based planner. The experiments show the superior
performance of our methods in comparison to the state-of-the-
art planners from the OMPL benchmark.

Abstract: The asymptotically optimal version of Rapidly- exploring Random Tree (RRT*) is often used to find optimal paths in a high-dimensional configuration space. The well-known issue of RRT* is its slow convergence towards the optimal solution. A possible solution is to draw random samples only from a subset of the configuration space that is known to contain configurations that can improve the cost of the path (omniscient set). A fast convergence rate may be achieved by approximating the omniscient with a low-volume set. In this paper, we propose new methods to approximate the omniscient set and methods for their effective sampling. First, we propose to approximate the omniscient set using several (small) hyperellipsoids defined by sections of the current best solution. The second approach approximates the omniscient set by a convex hull computed from the current solution. Both approaches ensure asymptotical optimality and work in a general n-dimensional configuration space. The experiments have shown superior performance of our approaches in multiple scenarios in 3D and 6D configuration spaces. The proposed methods will be available as open-source on https://github.com/BipoaroXigen/JPL.
